newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Ex-Soviet republics give muted reaction to union.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Soviet republics give muted reaction to union.

text.p: Russia's opposition communists swallowed their pride to applaud the Union Treaty with Belarus signed by President Boris Yeltsin on Wednesday, but the other former Soviet republics were largely silent.
Russian Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, usually one of Yeltsin's main foes, called the signing of the treaty "the most sober step by President Boris Yeltsin over the past five years".
"I congratulate you all," he told a news conference. "We live in a Union again...which stretches from Brest (on the Polish border) to Vladivostok (in the Far East)."

Liberals in Moscow were less happy with the treaty but were relieved that last-minute bargaining watered it down to reduce what they saw as the threat of Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko gaining a say in decisions affecting Russia.

Belarussian nationalists and protesters who fear Belarus will eventually lose its sovereignty showed their opposition by marching through Minsk. Witnesses said about 100 people were detained and some were hurt after clashes with police.
There was no sign of celebrating in the other former Soviet republics. None responded publicly to a clause in the treaty saying the union was open to other countries.
The newly independent states, on their own since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, have said they favour the idea of closer ties in principle with other former Soviet republics.
But they caution against hasty moves and fear any steps that might allow Moscow to gain domination over them again.
Ukraine, the third Slav state in the former Soviet Union, offered no official reaction on Wednesday.

But Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma said on Monday he regarded unification by individual countries within the Commonwealth of Independent States, formed on the ashes of the Soviet Union, as "a way to the destruction of the CIS."

Uzbek President Islam Karimov said last week: "One should not force processes which have not matured. We create problems for ourselves by signing documents which are clearly not ready and insufficiently justified."
Kazakhstan, Russia's Central Asian neighbour, was cautious on Wednesday.

Krymbek Kusherbayev, President Nursultan Nazarbayev's spokesman, said Kazakhstan was happy to see a union between Russia and Belarus, but was concerned by some aspects of the treaty and by the speed of its adoption.

"Instead of working for the cause of unification, the union treaty may cause disagreements within Russia. A number of Russia's regions, Chechnya, for example, may demand a similar treaty for themselves," he said.

Kazakhstan is worried by separatism in Russia and the possible consequences of the treaty for trade disputes it has with Moscow and for documents on cooperation that have not yet been ratified by Moscow.
Moldova has moved towards closer cooperation with Ukraine in recent weeks, but it welcomed the Belarus-Russia union.
"The union between Russia and Belarus does not contradict international norms," President Petru Lucinschi said.
Latvia, one of the three former Soviet republics not in the CIS, appeared to take a public stance typical of the former Soviet republics.
Latvia, which was swallowed against its will by the Soviet Union, said it did not oppose union between Moscow and Minsk but would keep a close eye on further integration moves.

"In practice...we cannot have anything against it," Latvian Foreign Minister Valdis Birkavs was quoted as saying by Itar-Tass news agency. "We are watching closely what has been happening and how it will affect earlier accords."
